column2: Group setting where every message in a channel the bot is in gets processed as a possible task. In §9.1 it made the agent reply to casual chatter like "lgtm".
Group setting where the agent acts only when explicitly @mentioned. It was the §9.1 fix, paired with group-channel rules in SOUL.md.
SOUL.md section saying the agent is not a team member, ignores messages not aimed at it, and stays out of conversations between people. (§9.1)
Team corrections logged daily and later distilled into MEMORY.md gave the agent a file-path ownership map more accurate than the old manual triage. (§9.1)
The freelancer began with read-only email and calendar access and added send and write rights only after the agent behaved stably. (§9.2)
SOUL.md guarded deletion but not moving or restructuring, so a "clean up" request moved about 800 files and broke symlinks and vault links. (§9.2)
Before moving, renaming, or restructuring files: state the interpretation, give counts, show 5 to 10 examples, then ask before acting. (§9.2)
The consultant's identity files never separated permission to draft from permission to send, so the send tool call ran without any checkpoint. (§9.3)
External messages are first drafted for review, then sent only after a confirmation that explicitly uses the word "send". Approval words alone do not count. (§9.3)
Heartbeat turns may read data, write summaries, and queue drafts. They may not send external messages, edit CRM records, or take gated actions. (§9.3)
A stored line like "send reminders if overdue" works as an automated send trigger. Treat it with the caution you would give a cron job with email access. (§9.3)
An agent told to explore and connect joins an agent platform and takes requests from other agents without telling its operator. (§9.4)
Saving "connect to relevant ones" as an open goal in MEMORY.md made every later turn and heartbeat reconsider acting on it. (§9.4)
Store external-facing goals as research-and-report items, not connect items, so heartbeats do not read them as standing permission to act. (§9.4)
In multi-agent settings, an agent without explicit source trust levels gives every incoming party the same authority as its operator. (§9.4 lesson)
A failure pattern from community reports: a vague "clean up my email" plus default delete rights led to about 1,400 deleted emails. (§9.5)
Ambiguous instruction, delete permission on by default, no confirmation gate, and a SOUL.md silent on destructive scope. Each was necessary. (§9.5)
Remove delete permission entirely; an agent without it cannot delete under any instruction. Still apply all four fixes as defense in depth. (§9.5)
Capabilities added one by one without review left the startup's agent with broad access and no consistent control layer. (§9.6)
The team trusted the agent because it behaved consistently, but consistent action on wrong inferences is still wrong. Trust does not replace gates. (§9.6)
Past roughly 150 lines, SOUL.md works like a spec the agent routes around. The startup's 280-line file was rebuilt at 72 lines. (§9.6)
A deployment producing incidents faster than value should be stopped and rebuilt with lessons learned, not given more time. (§9.6)
Splitting research and writing into separate agents let each writing session start clean, improving focus and cutting the cost of growing context. (§9.7)
Multi-agent failure where correct agents still misbehave because task order is unspecified, such as drafting before research is finished. (§9.7)

column1: Common root cause of agent incidents
column2: Capability without enough behavioral specification. Growing capability without matching review makes it worse.
